paper_title: IF-MAP: Influence-Function-Inspired Agent Prioritization in Multi-Agent Systems

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Improving every agent in an LLM-based multi-agent system can be prohibitively costly, making it important to identify which agent should be prioritized to achieve the greatest system-level gain with limited resources. Failure attribution can inform this decision, but an agent's responsibility for failures does not directly reveal the system-level gains achievable by improving it. We therefore introduce IF-MAP, an influence-function-inspired method for identifying agents with high potential for system-level improvement. For each agent, IF-MAP measures end-to-end loss changes under controlled semantic prompt perturbations, fits a regularized local response model in a low-dimensional prompt-embedding subspace, and uses the estimated response norm as a priority score. This black-box procedure requires no access to model parameters or gradients and produces agent priorities that can guide subsequent improvement effort. We evaluate IF-MAP across six multi-agent workflows spanning code generation, question answering, and mathematical reasoning, using the same priorities for prompt optimization and model upgrades. Optimizing the selected agents' prompts achieves a macro-average gain of 3.81 percentage points, compared with 1.85 for uniform agent selection. Across five target models, upgrading the selected agents yields macro-average gains of 7.62-16.42 percentage points, compared with 3.81-8.62 for uniform agent selection. Despite its probing overhead, IF-MAP reduces Qwen3-8B and DeepSeek-V3.2 token use by 74.2% and 35.2%, respectively, relative to optimizing every agent, and reduces target-model tokens by 63.6-64.9% relative to upgrading every agent. These results support the use of IF-MAP to identify promising agents and direct improvement effort toward greater end-to-end performance gains.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems distribute complex tasks across specialized agents that generate solutions, gather evidence, coordinate reasoning, and verify intermediate or final outputs (Wu et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2025a). Their performance depends on both the capabilities of individual agents and the interactions through which their outputs affect the overall computation. Improving such system therefore offers several possible interventions: replacing an agents model with more capable one, fine-tuning its model, refining its instructions, or improving its tools. However, these interventions need not produce comparable benefits at different agents. For example, in question-answering workflow, refining the answer-generation agents prompt may improve overall answer accuracy, whereas refining the prompt of the agent that combines candidate answers may yield little benefit or even reduce accuracy. Determining where to direct improvement effort is consequently an important decision in developing multi-agent systems. This decision becomes particularly consequential under limited development compute, evaluation capacity, or deployment resources. Improving all agents may exceed these resource limits. For example, replacing every agents model with more capable one can substantially increase the inference cost of each workflow execution, making system-wide upgrade prohibitively expensive. 1 Preprint Figure 1: Overview of IF-MAP. Given fixed multi-agent system 1, we perturb one agents prompt at time and measure end-to-end losses on the probing set 2. Subspace ridge regression on normalized prompt-embedding displacements and loss responses estimates local response vector; its norm gives an influence-function-inspired priority score 3. We rank agents by this score 4 and direct improvement effort toward the top-ranked agent 5, e.g., through prompt revision, model upgrades, or fine-tuning. The ranking is illustrative. We therefore study agent prioritization: given fixed multi-agent system, select the agent whose improvement is expected to produce the largest end-to-end performance gain. This formulation captures the next improvement decision in an ongoing development process. The goal is to identify high-value target without carrying out the full improvement procedure for every candidate agent. Existing work provides useful foundations for this decision. Failure-attribution methods identify agents and execution steps associated with unsuccessful outcomes, providing evidence for debugging and system refinement (Zhang et al., 2025b). Nevertheless, responsibility for an observed failure does not uniquely determine an agents potential for system-level improvement. An agent may frequently contribute to errors while offering little room for improvement, whereas another agent may admit change that substantially improves downstream behavior. Intervention-oriented studies further demonstrate the importance of evaluating actual recovery and realized system-level gains (Ma et al., 2026; Yoon & Kim, 2026). These observations motivate complementary objective: estimating which agent is promising target for system-level improvement under limited budget. Influence functions offer useful conceptual starting point for this objective. Classical influence functions characterize how perturbations to training data affect learned model and its predictions (Koh & Liang, 2017). We take inspiration from this perturbation-based perspective and investigate whether controlled changes to an agent can reveal information useful for prioritizing its improvement. Because an agents outputs propagate through the remaining workflow, measuring the resulting end-to-end loss captures responses beyond that agents immediate behavior. In the black-box setting considered here, we obtain this evidence through workflow executions and semantic representations, without requiring access to model parameters or gradients. The central hypothesis is that an estimated local response can reveal agents with substantial improvement potential, providing useful signal for allocating improvement effort. We propose IF-MAP, Influence FunctionInspired Multi-Agent Prioritization for System Improvement. For each agent, IF-MAP constructs controlled semantic prompt perturbations and measures 2 Preprint Figure 2: Macro-average performance and ranking agreement across six workflows spanning code generation (HumanEval and MBPP), question answering (NQ, HotpotQA and DROP), and mathematical problem solving (MATH). The base model (before the model upgrade) is Qwen3-8B. Higher mean performance and ranking agreement (Kendall τb) indicate better system performance and stronger agreement between the agent-priority and realized-improvement rankings, respectively. their effects on end-to-end loss while keeping the remaining system configuration fixed. It represents these perturbations as displacements in prompt-embedding space and fits regularized local response model within low-dimensional subspace. The norm of the estimated response vector then provides an agent-priority score, incorporating both the observed loss changes and the geometry of the perturbations. Prompt perturbations serve as executable black-box interventions, and the resulting ranking guides subsequent improvement effort. This makes IF-MAP prioritization step that can be used alongside existing agent-improvement methods. The score uses estimated local response sensitivity to define model-implied local intervention opportunity, whose relation to realized gains we evaluate through prompt optimization and model upgrades. We evaluate IF-MAP across six task-specific multi-agent workflows spanning code generation, question answering, and mathematical reasoning. We assess the usefulness of the same agent priorities through prompt optimization and upgrades to stronger models. Under prompt optimization, IF-MAP achieves macro-average selected gain of 3.81 percentage points (pp), compared with 1.85 pp for uniform agent selection  (Table 1)  . Across five model-upgrade targets, the selected gains range from 7.62 to 16.42 pp, compared with 3.818.62 pp for uniform agent selection  (Table 2)  . The selected mean gains exceed the uniform-selection reference on all six workflows under prompt optimization and each model-upgrade target. The priorities also align with observed improvement gains: mean Kendall τb is 0.741 for prompt optimization and 0.7080.804 across the five model upgrades. These findings support IF-MAP as useful tool for directing improvement effort toward agents with substantial potential for system-level gains. Our contributions are threefold: Agent prioritization for system improvement. We formulate the selection of an agent to prioritize under limited budget in fixed multi-agent system, with expected end-to-end improvement as the target quantity. Influence-function-inspired response estimation. We introduce IF-MAP, black-box prioritization method that combines semantic perturbations, whole-system response measurements, and regularized local model to estimate agent response sensitivity. Empirical validation of agent priorities. We evaluate the same priorities across six workflows through prompt optimization and model upgrades, obtaining higher mean selected gains than uniform agent selection and measuring ranking agreement with observed improvement gains.

It uses only 3.634.1% of their DeepSeekV3.2 requests and 1.516.6% of their DeepSeek tokens, shifting computation from diagnostic-model calls to base-model workflow execution. The same effect is more consequential for downstream improvement. Compared with applying the same prompt optimizer to every agent, selecting one agent with IF-MAP uses 30.69% of the Qwen requests, 25.82% of the Qwen tokens, 57.16% of the DeepSeek requests, and 64.78% of the DeepSeek tokens. For model replacement, FullSwap (i.e., upgrading every agent to the target model) avoids the Qwen3-8B and DeepSeek selection overhead, but invokes the target model for every agent: it uses 2.613.16 times as many target-model requests and 2.752.85 times as many target-model tokens as IF-MAP. Thus, the practical benefit of prioritization is not simply fewer total calls, but concentrating optimization and target-model calls on single promising agent while using cheaper model to decide where that effort should be spent. Complete request and token counts are reported in Appendix Tables 1618. 4.4 ABLATION STUDY Table 3 reports two matched ablations, macro-averaged with equal weight across the six workflows. The scoring-rule variants use the same probes and realized intervention gains, changing only how probe responses are converted into priorities. The budget variants all use G-norm but retain three, five, or up to ten formal probes per agent (adopted by our main IF-MAP configuration). For model upgrades, each agents gain is averaged across all five target models before aggregation. Complete aggregation rules appear in Appendix D. Scoring-rule ablation. This ablation directly tests the Section 3.2 choice to fit geometry-aware local response rather than use magnitude-only summaries. Using identical probes and test outcomes, G-norm obtains the highest selected gains: 3.812 pp for prompt optimization and 12.394 8 Preprint pp for model upgrades, exceeding I-abs by 0.536 and 2.998 pp and MeanAbs by 0.236 and 3.304 pp, respectively. The larger model-upgrade advantage suggests that the direction and displacement information used by G-norm transfers beyond prompt editing. However, MeanAbs has slightly higher prompt-ranking agreement (0.774 versus 0.741) while yielding lower selected gain, showing that agreement over the full ranking need not identify the best top-ranked intervention target. Probe-budget comparison. With G-norm, increasing the budget from three to five probes raises selected gain from 2.452 to 2.903 pp for prompt optimization and from 6.744 to 7.806 pp for model upgrades, while mean Kendall τb increases by 0.126 for both. The full pool of up to ten probes further raises the gains to 3.812 and 12.394 pp and substantially improves ranking agreement, suggesting that five probes provide insufficient aggregate directional coverage. Per-workflow effects are not monotonic, and the reduced variants retain auxiliary adaptive evaluations; the comparison therefore supports larger formal response pool rather than proportional cost reduction.

sections.title: 5 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Attribution, debugging, and improvement. Failure-attribution and debugging methods localize agents or steps associated with unsuccessful outcomes through full-trajectory attribution, counterfactual blame, constraint-based evidence, and other localization signals (Zhang et al., 2025b; West et al., 2025; Shen et al., 2025; Barke et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026; Ge et al., 2025). We adapt six such methods as external selectors in Section 4.1. DoVer emphasizes that attribution should be validated through realized interventions (Ma et al., 2026). CICA shows more directly that, in its experimental setting, the module assigned the greatest responsibility is not necessarily the module whose repair yields the greatest benefit (Yoon & Kim, 2026). This distinction motivates our work: rather than equating responsibility with improvement potential, we evaluate workflow-level agent priorities through two downstream intervention families. Optimizing prompts and workflows. ProTeGi and TextGrad use textual feedback to improve prompts or compound computations (Pryzant et al., 2023; Yuksekgonul et al., 2025). AFlow searches executable agentic workflows (Zhang et al., 2025a). HiveMind uses coalition-based credit for online prompt optimization, while Agents that Matter studies removaland model-replacementbased attribution (Xia et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026). Their coalition/removal variants require semantics-preserving executor for workflows with absent agents, which is not consistently available for our workflows; Appendix gives details. Optimas instead optimizes components with globally aligned local rewards (Wu et al., 2026). Our work focuses on the preceding allocation decision of which agent to improve. Local response estimation. Our response-estimation procedure is methodologically related to local sensitivity analysis and finite-difference estimation (Borgonovo & Plischke, 2016; Nocedal & Wright, 2006), as well as local surrogate methods such as LIME (Ribeiro et al., 2016). These approaches characterize local inputoutput behavior through derivatives, perturbations, or locally fitted surrogate models. IF-MAP applies this general principle at the level of semantically structured agent responses: each perturbed response is propagated through the downstream workflow, and its effect on task-level system utility is measured to estimate an agent-level response signal. This signal is then used to prioritize candidate agents for improvement under fixed intervention budget. We demonstrate that the estimated priorities translate into practical gains through downstream interventions including prompt optimization and model upgrades.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduced IF-MAP, black-box method for deciding where limited improvement effort should be directed in fixed LLM-based multi-agent system. By measuring end-to-end responses to semantic prompt perturbations and fitting regularized local response model, IF-MAP estimates modelimplied local intervention opportunities and identifies agents with promising system-level improvement potential. Across six workflows, its priorities guide both prompt optimization and model upgrades, yielding larger selected gains than uniform agent selection while reducing the expensive 9 Preprint downstream calls required by full-agent interventions. These results suggest that local response estimation can provide practical link between failure analysis and resource-aware multi-agent system improvement. Realized gains depend on the embedding model, local linearity, probe coverage, and the alignment between available interventions and the fitted loss-reducing direction. Future work should translate the continuous response direction into discrete improvements through directionconditioned generation, iterative edit-and-measure procedures, adaptive probing, and uncertaintyaware selection. 10 Preprint

sections.content: The study uses existing public benchmarks and model services. Generated code can be unsafe and must be executed in an appropriately restricted environment. Execution transcripts may contain sensitive material in deployment settings; only authorized data should be sent to external promptgeneration or judgment services. Scientific integrity requires retaining infrastructure failures, distinguishing missing from zero results, and disclosing adaptations of published baselines.

sections.title: F EXTERNAL SELECTORS AND ADAPTATIONS
sections.content: The six external selectors use the same frozen DEV-A trajectories, node inventory, and downstream gain matrices. Diagnostic judgments use DeepSeek-V3.2, while task execution uses the base workflow model. Each selector is run independently three times. Valid task-level attributions are aggregated over failed development trajectories to form workflow-level node ranking; unparseable outputs and explicit abstentions contribute no vote. The resulting ranking is used unchanged for both prompt optimization and model upgrades. Who&When-AAO. We use the papers All-at-Once prompt, which reads the complete failed trajectory in one request and returns an agent, an error step, and reason. valid agentstep attribution contributes one vote to that agent. Votes are summed over failed trajectories to obtain the node ranking. A2P. One diagnostic request performs the papers three reasoning stages: abduction of the failure cause, minimal corrective action, and prediction of the resulting continuation. The final agent step attribution contributes one vote, and the workflow-level ranking is obtained by aggregating these votes. Adapted locator. We first apply the task critic adapted from the papers critic template to the final workflow output and its recorded evaluation evidence. The locator then uses this feedback together with agent roles and the complete trajectory to return set of weak agents. Each trajectory contributes one vote divided uniformly over that set, and the accumulated shares determine the ranking. We evaluate this localization component independently of the papers subsequent workflowoptimization stage. AgentRx. The recorded trajectory is converted to AgentRxs canonical intermediate representation. Its static and dynamic invariant generators produce checks, the generated Python and naturallanguage checks are evaluated, and the native judge assigns failure category and responsible step from the resulting violation log. Generated Python checks run in isolated containers. mapped responsible step contributes one vote to its owning agent; intermediate violation counts are not used as node scores. CHIEF. The implementation follows CHIEFs staged diagnosis: retrieval-augmented task decomposition, OTAR construction, subtask/agent/step dependency graphs, virtual oracle construction, hierarchical backtracking, and the final LocalPlanning-ControlData-FlowDeviation-Aware attribution. The final supported agent receives one task-level vote. The RAG store and the complete intermediate diagnosis are retained for every trajectory. FAMAS. For each failed anchor trajectory, the reported configuration combines the anchor with 20 additional replays and retains at most ten native leaf events per trajectory. The implementation abstracts events into agent/action/state triples, clusters semantically equivalent actionstate pairs within each agent, and applies the FAMAS frequency, coverage, and success/failure spectrum score with decay λ = 0.9. The owner of the unique highest-scoring anchor triple receives one vote; top-score tie produces an abstention. Why coalition/removal baselines are not included. HiveMind assigns node credit from coalition values on workflow DAG using Shapley calculation (Xia et al., 2026). Agents that Matter likewise formalizes agent credit through explicit removal protocols, alongside separate modelreplacement analysis (Lu et al., 2026). In the five chain-structured workflows used here, the current executable interface admits only the complete source-to-sink coalition: removing an intermediate node leaves downstream node without its required input. Under this coalition set, every node receives the same value v(N )/N , so the selected node is determined only by tie breaking. MATH admits additional graph-valid coalitions, but its composite operators do not define what downstream node should receive when one of its required parents is absent. Filling those inputs with null values or replaying outputs from the complete workflow would define different intervention rather than execute the coalition being evaluated. sections.title: I ARTIFACT PROVENANCE AND REPRODUCIBILITY
sections.content: All reported performance values are produced by the protocol specified in this appendix. The experimental records contain the three prioritization runs, five intervention runs, and the gain matrix used for each table. The following materials and evaluations support complete artifact release and broader replication. 1. Example IDs, generated prompt texts, perturbation omissions, response caches by repeat, and the gain matrix used for each table. 2. Per-call query, token, latency, and monetary accounting for the prioritization methods and downstream interventions. 3. Evaluations on independently constructed workflows with different interaction graphs and additional intervention families. 4. public artifact at https://github.com/s1412/IF-MAS containing the prompt snapshots, dependencies, evaluation commands, and applicable licenses. Future topology studies could include code generation with execution feedback, question decomposition with evidence checking, and independent mathematical solution verification. Workflows with distinct interaction graphs would test whether node-response score remains useful when information routing and correction opportunities change.
